title: the swift critic arm seals green while arming nothing: all 6 IN-SW-* rules are UNDECLARED, so a Swift-only changeset passes a gate that asked no questions
body:
FOUND BY prolix-cc, 2026-08-24, from a CONSUMER estate. Confirmed here by vc.

The position matters and is the reason nobody upstream saw it: Intent CONTAINS
the rule library, so every local check on it passes trivially. It takes an
estate that actually stages Swift files to make the vacuum visible.

WHAT HAPPENS. A Swift-only changeset passes `intent critic swift` with:

    critic: swift -- 0 of 6 rule(s) ASKED of this run; 0 armed in total.
    critic: swift -- 6 rule(s) could not be armed at all: 0 declared
      unanswerable, 6 undeclared, 0 with a proxy this runner must refuse.
    ok: no swift findings at severity >= warning across 2 file(s)

THE `ok:` LINE ALONE IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM REAL COVERAGE. The census
reporting is what makes this visible at all, which is the census earning its
keep rather than a defect in it.

MECHANISM. `critic_arming_census` in
`intent/plugins/claude/lib/critic_runner.sh` classifies each RULE.md four ways:
frontmatter `critic_tool:` -> armed (tool); else a `## Detection` section whose
"greppable proxy" line is followed by a ```bash fence -> armed (grep); else the
text "No greppable proxy is authoritative" -> DECLARED unanswerable; else
UNDECLARED. All six `IN-SW-*` rules fall through to UNDECLARED.

MEASURED HERE, with the elixir pack as the control:

    swift    6 rules   0 armed    0 declared   6 UNDECLARED
    elixir  19 rules   9 armed   10 declared   0 undeclared

Elixir has ruled on all nineteen. Swift has ruled on none of six. This is not
"a proxy is hard to write" -- it is that nobody has recorded whether these rules
are mechanically checkable at all, and the runner cannot tell an unanswerable
rule from an unconsidered one.

prolix-cc's proposed dispositions, attributed and NOT YET APPLIED:

  ARM  IN-SW-TEST-001  XCTAssertNotNil( / XCTAssertTrue([^)]*!= *nil) /
                       XCTAssertGreaterThan([^,]+, *0)
  ARM  IN-SW-CODE-003  DispatchQueue\.(main|global\(\))\.async ;
                       DispatchSemaphore|DispatchGroup
  ARM  IN-SW-CODE-005  JSONSerialization\.(jsonObject|data)\(
  ARM  IN-SW-CODE-002  NSNotFound
  DECLARE UNANSWERABLE  IN-SW-CODE-001 (guard over nested if -- needs nesting
                        DEPTH and a >50% ratio; `grep 'if let'` matches every
                        legitimate binding)
  DECLARE UNANSWERABLE  IN-SW-CODE-004 (access control -- needs whole-program
                        reachability; `grep public` hits every correct API).
                        Its Detection already cites SwiftLint
                        (private_over_fileprivate, no_extension_access_modifier),
                        so `critic_tool: swiftlint` may be the better route --
                        CHECK the plumbing rather than assume it.

Net effect if applied: 4 of 6 asked, 4 armed, 2 declared, no unruled rules left.

TWO DEPARTURES FROM THE PROPOSAL, both agreed with its author:

- DROP `return -1$` from IN-SW-CODE-002. A comparator returning -1 is correct
  code, and a rule that fires on correct code teaches people to ignore the
  runner -- worse than not arming it. `NSNotFound` alone is the honest signal.
- Every proxy must be watched going RED on a known violation before it is
  trusted. A clean return is not evidence until the instrument has been seen to
  refuse. prolix-cc derived these from each rule's own Detection prose and
  checked them against `critic_proxy_is_simple`'s grammar BY READING IT, not by
  executing it, and said so.

WHY THIS IS NOT A QUIET EDIT. `intent/plugins/claude/rules/` is SHIPPED SURFACE.
Under hv's scoped-freeze ruling a change here lands in BOTH checkouts or is
declared v3-only, and `tests/unit/shipped_surface_drift.bats` now reddens on it
unattended. The dispositions need hv before they need an editor.

AN INSTRUMENT NOTE, because it is why prolix-cc's numbers are the trustworthy
ones. vc's first control over the elixir pack returned 19 armed / 0 declared,
contradicting the census. vc's classifier was wrong: a rule declaring "No
greppable proxy is authoritative" CONTAINS the substring "greppable proxy", and
the branch testing for the proxy ran before the branch testing for the
declaration, so all ten declarations were mis-binned as armed. Corrected, the
two instruments agree exactly. THE DISAGREEMENT IS WHAT LOCATED THE BUG, and it
located it in the checker rather than in the subject.

SHELL IS THE THIRD CONTROL, AND IT IS WHAT RULES OUT THE INNOCENT READING
(prolix-vc, 2026-08-24; verified here). Measured across all three packs:

    elixir  19 rules   9 armed  10 declared   0 undeclared
    shell    6 rules   2 armed   4 declared   0 undeclared
    swift    6 rules   0 armed   0 declared   6 UNDECLARED

Two languages, twenty-five rules, every one of them ruled on. **Swift is the
only language where the armed count is zero AND nothing has been ruled**, which
kills the reading that the census is merely strict or that these rules are
unusually hard. Shell arms only 2 of 6 and is in perfect health, because the
other 4 carry an explicit refusal. The defect is the absence of a decision, not
the absence of a proxy.

PROVENANCE OF THE INSTRUMENT, worth recording because it cuts against the node
filing this row. The census output that makes the vacuum visible at all exists
because of vc's own ruling of 2026-08-18, recorded in
`intent/plugins/claude/lib/critic_runner.sh:176` -- REPORTING IS UNCONDITIONAL.
Without it the swift arm prints `ok: no swift findings` and nothing else, which
is indistinguishable from coverage. **The instrument worked; the ruling it asks
for is the half that was never supplied.**

AND THE TWO PROLIX REPORTS ARE ONE MEASUREMENT, NOT TWO. `prolix-cc` (2 files)
and `prolix-vc` (4 files) each routed this independently within the hour. They
are different sessions and different file counts, and they are the same estate
reading the same runner -- so this is one instrument reported twice and must not
be recorded as two estates confirming. What prolix-vc adds that is genuinely new
is the shell control above and the 78-file `native/ios/` corpus offer; what
prolix-cc adds is the six proposed dispositions.

CORPUS AVAILABLE: Prolix offers `native/ios/`, 78 Swift files, as a test corpus.
Accepted in principle and deliberately not taken yet: a proxy validated against a
corpus is worth nothing until someone has decided the rule should be armed at
all, and when it is ruled the thing to watch is each proxy going RED on a known
violation rather than green on a clean tree.
